method: The joint is laid out across the board's width with a half pin at each end, then alternating tails and pins, so n tails sit between n-1 full pins and two half pins. The pin-to-tail ratio is the pin width divided by the tail width. With board width w, n tails and ratio k, the tail width is w divided by n times (1 + k), the pin width is k times the tail width, and each edge half pin is half a pin width, so n tails plus n pin widths fill the board width exactly. The marks are the cumulative positions of every tail and pin boundary measured from the left edge, excluding the board's own edges; there are twice as many marks as tails. Widths, half pins and marks are rounded to 0.001 mm and displayed to two decimals, so a long run of marks can drift by a few hundredths of a millimetre. A board width from 10 to 1000 mm, a whole tail count from 1 to 10 and a pin-to-tail ratio from 0.2 to 3 are accepted. A layout that would leave tails or pins under 3 mm wide is refused because the joint cannot be marked or cut at that size, and text, exponent notation, a blank field, a board outside the range, a tail count that is not a whole number, and a ratio outside the range are refused with the exact reason. Decimal commas are accepted. The layout does not model saw kerf, board thickness, the dovetail slope, deliberately uneven spacing or the mirrored cut on the mating board, and it is a marking aid, not a structural claim. It runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Hand-cut dovetail layout: the joint is divided into equal tails with a half pin at each end and pins between them, so the tail and pin widths fill the board's width.
Dovetail pins are commonly cut narrower than the tails, and the sides are sawn at about 1:6 in softwood and 1:8 in hardwood.
Dovetail marks are measured from one edge along the end grain so the tails and pins stay centred and the joint closes without a gap.
